lexemes.note: Used as a mass noun. Wiktionary’s English entry okra gives במיה (bamia, f.); there is no Hebrew entry.

profile.feeling: Okra in tomato sauce — a favourite of Jews from Iraq, Syria and Egypt; loved or found slimy.

examples.tr: Mom cooks okra in tomato sauce.

examples.text: אֲנִי לֹא אוֹהֵב בַּמְיָה, הִיא רִירִית מִדַּי.
examples.tr: I (m.) don’t like okra, it’s too slimy.
I bought frozen okra.

etymology.text: Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry. From Arabic بَامِيَة (bāmiya, “okra”), whose own origin is unknown (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The word is shared around the region: Arabic بَامِيَة, Turkish bamya, Greek μπάμια; English okra comes from a West African language, probably Igbo (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Feminine: בַּמְיָה טְרִיָּה.
A mass noun: “okra pods” is simply בַּמְיָה.
subtleties: To keep it less slimy, cooks add lemon or vinegar, or fry the okra before stewing it.

profile.feeling: Fresh green fava beans in spring; ful for breakfast.

examples.tr: In spring we shell fresh fava beans.
I (f.) buy a bag of dried fava beans.
Green fava beans are sweet when they are young.

synonyms.nuance: the Arabic pronunciation ful, especially for the cooked dish (Wiktionary: alternative form, from Arabic فُول)

etymology.text: Cognate with Aramaic פֹּולא (pōlā, “bean”) and Arabic فُول (fūl, “fava beans”). Ultimately perchance from Proto-Semitic *pūl- (“bean, corn, seed, grains, little pieces”).

funFacts: Arabic فُول (fūl) is the same word (Wiktionary); Egyptian ful medames is eaten all over the region.
People with G6PD deficiency (favism) — common in some Middle Eastern communities — must not eat fava beans.
pitfalls: Spelled like the name Paul (פּוֹל) and the slang פוּל “full, totally” — the context decides.
subtleties: Two pronunciations: pol (standard Hebrew) and ful (from Arabic, Wiktionary’s alternative form פוּל), which is the usual name of the cooked dish.

profile.feeling: A thistle eaten leaf by leaf; spring at the market.

examples.tr: She stuffs artichoke bottoms with meat.

examples.text: אֵיךְ אוֹכְלִים אַרְטִישׁוֹק? עָלֶה אַחֲרֵי עָלֶה.
examples.tr: How do you eat an artichoke? Leaf by leaf.
In spring there are artichokes at the market.

synonyms.nuance: the old name (via Babylonian Aramaic from Greek κινάρα), used in botany and learned style
a rarer synonym, close to Arabic خُرْشُوف (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: Ultimately from Italian articiocco, itself from Occitan artichaut, from Old Spanish alcarchofa, from Andalusian Arabic الْخَرْشُوف (al-ḵaršūf), from Arabic الْخُرْشُوف (al-ḵuršūf). Probably entered Hebrew through Russian артишок (artišok) and Yiddish אַרטישאָק (artishok).

funFacts: The European word comes from Arabic: الْخُرْشُوف → Spanish alcarchofa → Italian articiocco → English artichoke, Russian артишок — and Hebrew got it back through Russian and Yiddish (Wiktionary).
Greek αγκινάρα and the Hebrew synonym קִנְרָס both go back to Ancient Greek κινάρα (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: The article takes qamats before א: הָאַרְטִישׁוֹק, הָאַרְטִישׁוֹקִים.
Not the same as אַרְטִישׁוֹק יְרוּשַׁלְמִי (Jerusalem artichoke), a sunflower tuber.
subtleties: We eat the flower bud of a thistle: the fleshy base of its scales and the bottom (תַּחְתִּית).

lexemes.note: A loanword used as a mass noun. Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry.

profile.feeling: Crunchy and sweet, peeled and eaten raw as a snack.

examples.text: הַיְּלָדִים אוֹכְלִים קוֹלְרַבִּי חַי עִם מֶלַח.
examples.tr: The children eat raw kohlrabi with salt.
I (f.) make a kohlrabi salad.
This kohlrabi is big and hard.

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday synonym; the German name is used.

etymology.text: Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry. From German Kohlrabi, from Italian cavoli rape, plural of cavolo rapa (“cabbage-turnip”) (Wiktionary, German Kohlrabi).

funFacts: The name means “cabbage-turnip” (Italian cavolo rapa → German Kohlrabi), and that is what it is: a cabbage with a turnip-like stem.
pitfalls: It is not a root: the ball grows above the ground — it is a swollen stem.
Masculine: קוֹלְרַבִּי טָרִי.
subtleties: In Israel it is eaten mostly raw, peeled and sliced; in Central Europe it is more often cooked.

profile.feeling: Mini cabbages — loved roasted, hated boiled.

examples.text: אֲנִי צוֹלָה כְּרוּב נִצָּנִים בַּתַּנּוּר עִם שֶׁמֶן זַיִת.
examples.tr: I (f.) roast Brussels sprouts in the oven with olive oil.
The children don’t like Brussels sprouts.

examples.text: אֶת כְּרוּב הַנִּצָּנִים צָרִיךְ לַחְתֹּךְ לִשְׁנַיִם.
examples.tr: The Brussels sprouts have to be cut in half.

etymology.text: כְּרוּב “cabbage” (from Ancient Greek κράμβη) + נִצָּנִים, plural of נִצָּן “bud”: “bud cabbage”.

funFacts: Each sprout is a bud growing along a tall stem — hence “bud cabbage”; English names it after Brussels and German calls it Rosenkohl, “rose cabbage”.
pitfalls: A mass noun in Hebrew: כְּרוּב נִצָּנִים is “Brussels sprouts” (plural in English).
The article goes on the second word: כְּרוּב הַנִּצָּנִים. Everyday spelling with י: כרוב ניצנים.
subtleties: נִצָּנִים are buds or blossoms, as in the Song of Songs (2:12): הַנִּצָּנִים נִרְאוּ בָאָרֶץ, “the blossoms appear on the earth”.

profile.feeling: Mostly the bath sponge; as a vegetable only in Asian cooking.

senses.def: luffa, sponge gourd (the plant; its young fruit is eaten as a vegetable)
loofah — the dried fibrous fruit used as a bath sponge

examples.tr: He grows luffas in the garden.

examples.text: אֶת הַלּוּפָה אוֹכְלִים כְּשֶׁהִיא צְעִירָה וְרַכָּה.
examples.tr: The luffa is eaten when it is young and soft.
I have a loofah in the shower.

etymology.text: Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry. Like English loofah, which Wiktionary gives as “borrowed from Arabic لُوفَة (lūfa)”.

funFacts: The bath sponge is the dried fruit of this gourd — the same fruit you can eat while it is young.
pitfalls: To most Israelis לוּפָה is the bath sponge; say which one you mean.

lexemes.note: A recent loanword, used as a mass noun. Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry.

profile.feeling: A trendy superfood of the 2010s: crisp baked leaves and green smoothies.

examples.text: הִיא אוֹפָה עֲלֵי קֵייל בַּתַּנּוּר עַד שֶׁהֵם פְּרִיכִים.
examples.tr: She bakes kale leaves in the oven until they are crisp.
I (m.) add kale to the salad.
Kale is considered a very healthy food.

profile.synonymsNone: No established Hebrew synonym; the English name came with the trend.

etymology.text: Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry. From English kale (from Old English cāl, from Latin caulis “stalk, cabbage”; Wiktionary).

funFacts: English kale and German Kohl go back to Latin caulis; Wiktionary even lists English gobi (from Hindi gobhī “cabbage, cauliflower”) among its doublets.
pitfalls: Pronounced keil, as in English; masculine: קֵייל טָרִי.
A young word: older dictionaries do not have it.
subtleties: Raw kale is often massaged with oil and lemon to soften it.

profile.feeling: Pale, crinkly, mild leaves for stir-fries and kimchi.

examples.tr: He chops Chinese cabbage for the salad.
There are big Chinese cabbages at the supermarket.

examples.text: הַכְּרוּב הַסִּינִי רַךְ וּמָתוֹק יוֹתֵר מֵהַכְּרוּב הָרָגִיל.
examples.tr: Chinese cabbage is softer and sweeter than ordinary cabbage.

funFacts: Korean kimchi is usually made from this cabbage.
German calls it Chinakohl and Russian пекинская капуста, “Peking cabbage”.
pitfalls: Plural agreement: כְּרוּבִים סִינִיִּים; Wiktionary also lists the shorter סִינִים, the usual word for Chinese people.
In English “Chinese cabbage” can also mean bok choy; in Israeli shops כְּרוּב סִינִי is the elongated Napa cabbage.
subtleties: Both words take the article: הַכְּרוּב הַסִּינִי.

ref.src: Composed from the Wiktionary (kaikki.org) entries כְּרוּב and אָדֹם (no entry for the phrase)

profile.feeling: Purple crunch in salads; it changes colour with vinegar.

examples.text: אֲנִי מְכִינָה סְלַט כְּרוּב אָדֹם עִם לִימוֹן.
examples.tr: I (f.) make red cabbage salad with lemon.

examples.text: הַכְּרוּב הָאָדֹם מְשַׁנֶּה צֶבַע עִם חֹמֶץ.
examples.tr: Red cabbage changes colour with vinegar.
We bought two red cabbages.

etymology.text: כְּרוּב “cabbage” (from Ancient Greek κράμβη) + אָדֹם “red” (compare Classical Syriac ܐܕܘܡ, Arabic ادوم).

funFacts: Its juice is a natural pH indicator: red with acid, blue-green with soap or baking soda — a classic school experiment.
In southern Germany and Austria it is Blaukraut, “blue cabbage”; elsewhere Rotkohl, “red cabbage”.
pitfalls: Agreement and article on both words: הַכְּרוּב הָאָדֹם, כְּרוּבִים אֲדֻמִּים.
Everyday spelling with ו: כרוב אדום, כרובים אדומים.
subtleties: The article takes qamats before א: הָאָדֹם, הָאֲדֻמִּים.

profile.feeling: Sweet bite-size tomatoes in every lunch box and salad.

examples.tr: The children love cherry tomatoes.
The cherry tomatoes are cut in halves.
I bought a box of cherry tomatoes.

synonyms.nuance: short for the whole phrase in casual speech (סָלָט עִם שֶׁרִי); Wiktionary records שֶׁרִי only inside עַגְבָנִיַּת שֶׁרִי

etymology.text: עַגְבָנִיָּה “tomato” + שֶׁרִי, borrowed from English cherry, with original צֶ׳רִי (chéri) undergoing dissimilation or reanalysis due to the preceding ת (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew says sheri, not cheri: after the t of עַגְבָנִיַּת the English ch was simplified (Wiktionary).
Cherry tomatoes are not an Israeli invention, as is often claimed; Israeli breeders developed long-lasting varieties that helped make them a supermarket staple.
pitfalls: In the plural the first word changes and שֶׁרִי stays: עַגְבָנִיּוֹת שֶׁרִי; the article goes on שֶׁרִי: עַגְבָנִיּוֹת הַשֶּׁרִי.
Pronounced sheri, not cheri.
subtleties: Everyday spelling of the construct form with double י: עגבניית שרי.

lexemes.note: As food, mostly in the plural נְבָטִים “(bean) sprouts”. Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry.

profile.feeling: Crunchy white sprouts in stir-fries and spring rolls.

senses.def: sprout; as food (mostly plural נְבָטִים): bean sprouts
a sprout, a shoot coming out of any seed

examples.tr: He adds bean sprouts to the stir-fry.
These sprouts are fresh and crunchy.

examples.text: הַיְּלָדִים מְגַדְּלִים נְבָטִים שֶׁל שְׁעוּעִית בַּגַּן.
examples.tr: The children grow bean sprouts at kindergarten.
A small sprout came out of the seed.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; the kind is added in a construct phrase: נִבְטֵי מָשׁ, נִבְטֵי סוֹיָה.

etymology.text: Wiktionary (kaikki.org) gives no etymology for this word. It belongs to the root נ־ב־ט “to sprout” (נָבַט “sprouted”, נְבִיטָה “germination”).

funFacts: Chinese 豆芽 (dòuyá) literally means “bean sprout”, like נִבְטֵי שְׁעוּעִית.
The same root gives נְבִיטָה “germination” and הֵנְבִּיט “to make sprout”.
pitfalls: As food it is used in the plural: נְבָטִים; the singular נֶבֶט is one sprout.
subtleties: A segolate noun: the vowels change in the plural, נֶבֶט → נְבָטִים, like גֶּזֶר → גְּזָרִים.

lexemes.note: Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry; its English entry butternut squash gives דָּלוֹרִית (dalorít, f.).

profile.feeling: Sweet orange flesh for velvety soups and roasting; an autumn favourite.

examples.tr: I (f.) cook butternut squash soup.
He roasts butternut cubes in the oven.
In autumn butternut squashes are cheap at the market.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; other squashes are called דְּלַעַת.

etymology.text: Wiktionary has no Hebrew entry and gives no etymology; its English entry butternut squash (“Cucurbita moschata cultivar”) lists דָּלוֹרִית (dalorít) as the Hebrew word.

funFacts: English names it after butter and nuts; Hebrew gave this one squash variety a one-word name of its own.
pitfalls: Feminine: דָּלוֹרִית מְתוּקָה; plural דָּלוֹרִיּוֹת.
Not every orange squash is a דָּלוֹרִית: the general word is דְּלַעַת.
subtleties: The plural doubles the י, as with כְּרוּבִית → כְּרוּבִיּוֹת.

ref.src: Composed from the Wiktionary (kaikki.org) entries אֲפוּנָה and סִינִי (no entry for the phrase)

profile.feeling: Flat green pods, crisp in Asian stir-fries.

examples.text: הוּא מַקְפִּיץ אֲפוּנָה סִינִית עִם שׁוּם.
examples.tr: He stir-fries snow peas with garlic.

examples.text: אוֹכְלִים אֶת הָאֲפוּנָה הַסִּינִית עִם הַתַּרְמִיל.
examples.tr: Snow peas are eaten pod and all.
I bought snow peas at the market.

etymology.text: אֲפוּנָה “pea(s)” (Wiktionary gives no etymology) + סִינִית “Chinese”, feminine of סִינִי (סין “China” + ־י).

funFacts: French mangetout means “eat-all” — you eat the whole pod, as the Hebrew example says.
pitfalls: The adjective is feminine like אֲפוּנָה: אֲפוּנָה סִינִית, הָאֲפוּנָה הַסִּינִית.
A mass noun: “snow peas” is singular in Hebrew.
subtleties: On its own סִינִית means “Chinese (language)” or “a Chinese woman”; here it is only an adjective.
